newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian budget worsens A$3 billion.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian budget worsens A$3 billion.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello revealed on Tuesday that the budget outlook had worsened by almost A$3 billion and said the government would now aim to balance its books one year later than first planned.

But the A$7 billion budget tightening that the government implemented last year represented the bulk of necessary savings and he ruled out finding as much as the A$4 billion needed to balance the budget year from July 1997, as originally planned.
Economic forecasts were little changed, and 1996/97 GDP growth is still projected at 3.5 percent, with underlying inflation a little lower at two percent by mid 1997.
But Costello's latest Treasury estimates showed the projected 1996/97 fiscal deficit had blown out to A$8.5 billion from the A$5.6 billion he projected in the August budget.
"Company tax collections in 1996/97 are running significantly below budget-time estimates," he said in the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.

However, budgets for following fiscal years are also heading for deeper deficits than projected previously -- A$3.9 billion in 1997/98 instead of A$1.5 billion, and A$2.2 billion in 1998/99 instead of A$1.0 billion.

The government originally planned to close the 1997/98 budget gap, but Costello told reporters: "In this budget according to our forward estimates that would require a fiscal tightening of about A$4 billion.
"And I think I can assure you that I wouldn't lose any time at all looking for that," he said.
"What we're talking about is getting to balance over the life of the parliament (due to end in 1999), certainly not in the next financial year," he said.

The August budget announced A$7.2 billion in savings, of which the government lost about A$400 million when the upper house of parliament, the Senate, refused to pass the necessary legislation late last year.

Costello repeated the government's earlier statements that it accepted A$200 million of the Senate rejection as irredeemably lost but would put the other A$200 million back before the Senate again this year for a re-think.

The Australian budget has repeatedly underperformed Treasury forecasts in the 1990s, often because the government is disappointed when unexpectedly low inflation fails to lift workers into higher tax brackets.
Costello himself revealed an earlier collapse in budget forecasts when the Liberal-National coalition gained office last March.
He said then that the 1997/98 underlying budget -- that is, excluding asset sales -- would be A$8 billion and he responded with A$7 billion in cuts.
If that programme had not been implemented the 1997/98 budget would be heading for an A$11.2 billion deficit even after seven years of economic growth, Treasury's figures showed on Tuesday.
Although most economic forecasts were little changed, the government revised up its projection for the mid-1997 unemployment rate, to 8.5 percent from 8.2 percent.
Most economists had expected the new forecast to be even higher.

Price pressures eased. While the mid-1997 underlying inflation rate, which excludes large irregular items, fell to 2.0 percent from 2.75 percent, overall price rises were seen at just 1.0 percent, down from the originally forecast 2.0 percent.
The government revised up its 1996/97 business investment forecast to 17 percent from the already robust 14 percent projected in the budget.
